name: Soft Blue
lede: Soft blue is a plain description, not a defined color, and the books use it for pale and hazy blues: dyes, minerals and distant air.

sections.title: A description with history
sections.body:
Paterson records Nattier blue as a very soft blue used by Jean Nattier, who lived from 1685 to 1766 [1]. Balfour-Paul notes that the draperies and tapestries of better-off medieval houses were awash with soft blues or greeny-blues [2].

Minerals use the phrase too: georgeite, a copper carbonate, forms soft blue surface crusts [3]. Gurney explains a sky effect: a black card or piece of velvet held near a distant window looks infused with soft blue or violet, because air scatters light between you and the object [4]. The sky color is scattering, not a pigment [4]. Because it describes a quality, softness, more than a hue, it covers many blues and no single recipe [1][2][3]. Treat it as a way of talking about gentle blues in painting, dye and sky alike [1][2][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch #6488EA is a light, clear cornflower-like blue [5]. Its neighbors include [[periwinkle]], [[azure]] and [[light-blue]] [5]. Screen colors are approximate [5].

notes.cite: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, "Nattier blue", p. 275
